en: Regarding the supplementary commentary on the subtle nuances of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,

it is traditionally transmitted that the title includes the two characters "Buddha-spoken" (*bōshuō*), such that it is called the *Buddha-spoken Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth. This was added by later generations.
This is an erroneous addition. One must know that sūtras are spoken by five types of persons: namely, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, disciples, celestial beings (devas), and manifested persons.
If a section within a sūtra is spoken by four of these types, the title does not designate it as "spoken by the Buddha.
If a sūtra from beginning to end is spoken from the golden mouth [of the Buddha], the title bears the designation "Spoken by the Buddha" to distinguish it from those spoken by the other four types.

It is indeed spoken [by others]. However, why is it called a *sūtra*? One must understand that although these were spoken by four individuals, because they have been authenticated (*mudrā*) by the Buddha, they are identical to the Buddha’s own speech;
therefore, they may be called *sūtras*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The latter four [categories] are authenticated and are generally termed the Buddha’s teaching.
If this is so, and since they are generally termed the Buddha’s teaching, what is wrong with titling them "Spoken by the Buddha"? One must understand that they are generally termed the Buddha’s...
Only that which is spoken by the Golden Mouth may be called a Sūtra; were it not for what was spoken by the Golden Mouth, there would be but a single session [of teaching].

Furthermore, this sūtra has six translations in total. Among them, those by Master Kumārajīva, Bodhiruci of the Wei dynasty, and Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty—these three translations—are all titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth. As for the translation by Jñānagupta of the Sui dynasty, it is titled *Vajra*...

Regarding the *Nengduan* (The Severer): the Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang and the [Master] Yijing of the Great Zhou both translated this same work under the title *Nengduan Jingang Banruo* (The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā that Severes).
Thus, it is due to these differences in the titles established for them that their exegeses of the meaning differ.
Paramārtha [Guṇabhadra] used the two characters "able to sever" (*prabheda*) following the word "vajra";

thus, he took the "adamantine hardness and sharpness" to metaphorically represent *prajñā*, stating that "the adamantine able-to-sever *prajñā*" serves as the title for this Dharma teaching. This was the case with Master Xuanzang and Yijing.
The two characters "Able-to-Sever" (Nengduan) appear before "Vajra. As it is said, "the Bodhisattva’s firm adherence is like a vajra";
because one can sever this adherence by means of the emptiness-wisdom (*prajñā*) of *prajñā*, it is called the "Able-to-Sever Vajra Prajñāpāramitā" (as in the *Cien Zhuan*).
Thus, it constitutes a title established based on a single dharma. Since the emptiness-wisdom of *prajñā* is taken as the "able-to-sever" agent and the vajra as the object...

[The title] "Severance" (Duan) is indeed not a mere single dharma. It is traditionally said that the Korean master Hyo also produced a commentary on this sutra, which accords with the teachings of Master Xuanzang;
yet neither is to be adopted. The *Treatise of Asaṅga* establishes its title through both dharma and metaphor, and Master Kumārajīva and others all conformed to the intent of that treatise.
It cannot be consumed even by a hundred refinements.
One must know that this applies not only to vajra, but even to the "Bīn-iron" of this world, which likewise cannot be consumed even after a hundred refinements (*Bǐtán*).
This demonstrates its uniqueness.

In contrast to the initial meaning, it is specifically presented in this sutra; therefore, it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). However, as for its relationship with the subsequent text, the textual characteristics differ, and thus they cannot be treated as a single uniform case.

Pāramitā. In the Sanskrit language, *pāra* means "the other shore" (*bī'àn*, 彼岸), and *mitā* means "to reach. If the phrasing were reversed to conform to worldly convention, it would be called "reaching the other shore" (*dào bǐ'àn*, 到彼岸).
According to various texts, this is abbreviated as "three inversions. In most sutras, it is translated as "reaching the other shore. It gives rise to... [text ends]
Birth-and-death is this shore; nirvāṇa is the other shore; the afflictions are the middle current.

The bodhisattva, by means of the wondrous wisdom of signlessness, boards the vessel of meditative concentration and crosses from this shore of birth-and-death to that shore of nirvāṇa, or else turns back until the task is completed.
As stated in the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*: "According to the linguistic conventions of India, whenever a task is completed, one says 'pāramitā.
It may be translated as 'crossing over' (*du*) or 'infinite' (*wújí*). This term encompasses both profound and far-reaching meanings regarding both phenomena and principle.
Taken together, it is called 'crossing over the infinite' (*dù wújí*). Here, 'infinite' refers to the fulfillment of practice in terms of both phenomena and principle."
The three and one are both general and particular;
however, the general and the particular should not be mentioned simultaneously. This is like the analogy of a fist and fingers:

when speaking of the general, the general contains no particulars, for the general is formed by encompassing the particulars, just as when fingers are joined to form a fist, there is only the fist and no separate fingers. When speaking of the particular, the particular contains no further particulars. Particularity...
The general is opened up into the particular, just as a fist is opened into fingers; once the fingers are distinct, there is no longer a "fist" [as a separate entity].

If this is so, how can both the general and the particular coexist? Is it not a case of "one" being the general and "three" being the particular? One must understand that "One" is the general title, which provides a comprehensive overview of the great meaning of the entire sutra.

Thus, within the title, the meanings of essence (*tattva*), purpose (*prayojana*), and function (*kriyā*) are contained; therefore, it is called "general. "Three," on the other hand, refers to the specific aspects of what is explained.
The term "particular" (*bie*) refers to the fact that this specific passage elucidates the essence (*ti*), the thesis (*zong*), and the function (*yong*).
Since there are these two paths—textual and doctrinal—it is said that the "three and one" are both general and particular, allowing them to be mentioned together.

Maitreya. Maitreya is titled "The Benevolent One" (Maitreya). As it is said in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra: "Some see Maitreya first realizing the samādhi of the mind of loving-kindness;
from that time forth, he has been titled 'The Benevolent One'."
With what intention did he further compose this treatise to provide an exposition of the eighteen stages (*aṣṭādaśāvasthā*) of the sūtra?
Regarding the "Pure Awakening" (*Vimalabuddhi*), it is said that the eighty verses found following the *Aṣṭādaśāvasthā-śāstra* are not [the original work].
The Tripiṭaka Master Yijing stated: "In the West, there are many commentaries on this sūtra. Examining its origins, these verses are the earliest; thus, the eight..."
Ten verses. The matter must pertain to the correct [teaching].
It is also as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "He rose calmly from samādhi. Although it is not explicitly stated, the matter must pertain to the correct [teaching].
Correct. Three doubts arise with apprehension;

they are the opposite of what has been held since antiquity. There are two types of doubt: the general and the specific. First, regarding the general doubt: since the collection of the one thousand [sūtras] is...

Doubting the Arhat: Why is there doubt? As for specific doubts: first, since the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaches the extinction of the ashes [of the skandhas], how could they doubt that the Śākya-muni has reappeared?
Since the Small Vehicle has no discourse regarding other Buddhas, how could they doubt that a Buddha from another direction has come?
Since the Small Vehicle allows no portion for becoming a Buddha, how could they doubt that Ānanda will attain Buddhahood? Now...
To provide an explanation: regarding general doubt, an Arhat has no uncertainty concerning the principle of the Four Noble Truths, yet they lack full understanding of specific phenomena;
therefore, they possess doubt. For example, an Arhat might not recognize red salt and the like.

Regarding specific doubt, it is said that [the Buddha] does not exist because the Lesser Vehicle teachings do not elucidate him. As for the reason he harbors doubt, it is due to Kāśyapa’s prostration.
A thousand arhats were born of this veneration; each harbored hesitation and doubt, collectively possessing these three [states of mind].

This does not mean they were voicing what they themselves had already suspected. (Furthermore, even those of the Hīnayāna knew that there are Buddhas in other directions; however, they held that one Buddha transforms only a single region, and did not know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are all emanations of Śākyamuni.

Thus, they spoke of "no other Buddhas. These are the words from Siming’s letter to Yang Dainian. From ancient times, some have claimed that these "provisional doubts" were intended to initiate what was to come.
Regarding those who come with sincerity and faith: if that were so, Ānanda would have been expelled; yet this is clearly stated in the sūtras and śāstras.
Furthermore, his re-entry into the cave is also explicitly recorded in the sūtras and śāstras. Why, then, do you claim not to see the account of his return?

Is it because the matter is not manifest, and thus you have devised a pretext out of doubt, or perhaps a genuine doubt, claiming that the assembly did not recognize him because his appearance resembled that of the Buddha?

Doubt. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, at the time of the council, Kāśyapa made a formal motion (*jñapti*) to harmonize the Saṃgha, and only then did Ānanda ascend the precious throne.
If this is so, who would not recognize that the high throne was Ānanda’s? Why, then, would one say "I do not know him" and harbor doubt? Moreover, the Buddha possesses a golden-hued body;
the great assembly would have understood it upon a single glance. If, however, one follows the *Vinaya-sūkṣma* (the *Saṃyuktāgama-vinaya*), [it is as follows...]

I have not yet seen the original text of that Vinaya. I suspect that when Ānanda performed the compilation, his appearance was so refined and spirited, and his deportment so similar to that of the Buddha, that the devas attended upon him as they would the World-Honored One; thus it is said he "resembled the Buddha."

Regarding the phrase "much learning is hearing things," one must understand that these two instances of the word "hearing" differ: "much learning" refers to knowing through hearing, which pertains to oneself; "hearing things" refers to hearsay, which pertains to others.
Neither looking upward nor downward, neither square nor bound.

"Not looking upward" means not looking up with the mouth to eat; it refers to gazing at the stars and constellations to divining good or bad fortune. "Not looking downward" means not looking down with the mouth to eat;
it refers to tilling the soil, digging the earth, and planting in fields and gardens. "Not square" means not being square with the mouth.
"Eating" refers to traveling to deliver messages and running about in all directions. "Not maintaining" refers to failing to maintain the four cardinal points correctly.
This refers to seeking sustenance through minor arts such as medicine, divination, and calculation; these four are called the four kinds of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Regarding the bowls offered by the Four Kings:
each of the Four Heavenly Kings presented a bowl. Because the Buddha was impartial, he accepted all the offerings together; they were subsequently struck together to form a single bowl.
Now there are four [reasons] for the alms bowl;
[the first is] to eliminate pride.
The Buddha was the son of King Śuddhodana; since he practiced begging for food, it is prescribed in the teachings that if he sees others...
When I, the Buddha, went on almsrounds, I was never disrespectful.

From the very beginning, there was the mind of vastness, which is the mind of great vows. "Vast" (hong) means "great" (da). All categories of sentient beings within the three realms and the four [continents]...

Those who are born all enter into the count of those saved by my great vows, and I bring them to extinction. For some to claim that they themselves are delivering sentient beings as the Tathāgata does is an error.
Indeed it is so.
"Only" (*vā*) means "yes," "certainly," or "in response. "Indeed" (*tathā*) means "acceptance.
One desires to examine what is correct in order to reject what is erroneous;
to examine the meaning of that correctness, it is necessary to employ a reductio ad absurdum (*prasanga*). If a bodhisattva does not give rise to [a mind] toward all sentient beings...

If all other phenomena are exactly like one's own essence, then because one has faith and understanding in the equality of self and others, how could there be any views of a self, a person, and so forth?
Such a one is truly a bodhisattva; thus, the mind is not inverted.
In the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* and other scriptures, it is said: "When the True Dharma perishes, that which is false is called 'True'—this is the time when the Buddha-dharma is extinguished.

When the three [jewels] do not manifest before one's eyes, this is the time when the Triple Gem has vanished. This must refer to the final period of the Dharma-ending age, known as the five-hundred-year era.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta* should be taken as the correct authority. Some claim that the "final five hundred years" refers to the five hundred years following the first millennium of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), treating it as the "latter" in contrast to the "former. This interpretation, however, contradicts the *Ratnakūṭa*.
The merit of deeds is fundamentally empty.
This fundamental emptiness is precisely the wondrous nature. If this is so, how can the subsequent passages compare it?
Even down to the single phrase at the very beginning of the title.
Since a portion of these [texts] equally elucidate the true reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa), how could it be that merit exists only within the four lines? The Great Master said:
"Beneath every phrase, the wondrous name is universally concluded; within every sentence, the essence is fully embodied. This may be known by analogy.
After attaining the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), one advances to abandon the six grades of desire-realm thought-moments (*cetanā*).
There are nine grades of thought-moments for the lower realms, which together moisten seven cycles of birth and death. As for the nine grades:

they consist of three major categories—superior, middling, and inferior—and each of these is further divided into three, thus forming nine. Consequently, a single grade of the "superior-superior" (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) can moisten two births. Superior...
The middle-upper, upper-middle, and middle-lower grades each moisten one lifetime; the middle-middle and lower-middle grades together moisten one lifetime.
This constitutes the abandonment of six grades, which is fully capable of moistening six cycles of birth and death, whereby one realizes the second fruit.

There are two kinds of Arhats: namely, those who possess both wisdom and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and those who possess wisdom alone. There are those who fall back and those who do not. If one who possesses both [wisdom and concentration] attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they do not fall back.

If one who possesses wisdom alone does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation, they will fall back. However, this refers only to the falling back of noble ones; there is ultimately no such thing as a noble one falling back from the state of a noble one.
A noble one may fall back to the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). This is like falling into a sand well: one reaches the bottom before coming to rest.
Thus, one who has regressed from the four fruits falls back to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and remains there, performing the deeds of one who has attained the first fruit.

Furthermore, such a regression occurs within the same lifetime and is not separated by another birth. Those who attain [the fruit] after having regressed are mostly those liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*).

Regarding the citation of the text in the treatise: there are two instances of such citations within the treatise. The first occurs in the section on the "sevenfold meaning" (*saptārtha*) concerning the characteristics of initiating practice;

the second occurs during the formal explanation of the sūtra, where the *Gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges sands) is used as the unit for phrasing. It is only by reading the text according to the treatise that one’s interpretation will be deemed appropriate.
It should be understood that the Buddha’s era constitutes a distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
As for these distinct characteristics, the three marks are each separate. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "When he first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, by his power he subdued Māra."

Having attained the ambrosia of extinction and realized the path of enlightenment, he turned the wheel of Dharma thrice throughout the great chiliocosm. That wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure;
that humans and devas have attained the Way serves as its witness. Thus, the Three Jewels appeared in the world.
Therefore, one should know that since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Three Jewels had been obscured and vanished, while humans and devas diminished and the three evil realms became filled.

[The section on] Fulfillment: It was only when Śākyamuni Tathāgata appeared in the world that the Three Jewels first emerged in the world; therefore, it is said, "Thus the Three Jewels appear in the world.
This refers to their distinct characteristics (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa*), which are designated in contrast to their single essence (*eka-rasa*).

Second, regarding the maintenance [of the teachings] after the passing [of the Buddha]: Following the Tathāgata’s attainment of enlightenment, he contemplated how to repay his mother’s kindness. His mother, Lady Māyā, had already...

Having entered parinirvāṇa, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There, for ninety days, the Tathāgata ascended to heaven to preach the Dharma to his mother, veiling the entire assembly so that none were made aware of it.
At that time, King Udayana, longing for the Buddha, used red sandalwood incense; then Viśvakarman manifested as a master craftsman to carve an image of the Tathāgata for the king. From [there...]
There was a sandalwood image of the Buddha here. When the ninety-day summer retreat had concluded, the Buddha manifested three jeweled stairways and descended from heaven.
At that time, the king and the people all came to welcome the Buddha; at that moment, the sandalwood image also emerged from its pedestal to come and welcome him.
The Tathāgata then stroked the crown of the sandalwood image’s head and said: "After my parinirvāṇa, you shall maintain and uphold [the Dharma]."
Throughout the world, he extensively performed Buddha-work for the sake of humans and devas; from this time on, the title of "Abbot" (zhuchi) came into existence.
King Ajātaśatru, having committed a grave transgression, suffered the eruption of sores upon his body. At the assembly of the Parinirvāṇa, he encountered the Buddha and heard the Dharma;

his sores were immediately healed, and he attained the patience of rootless faith (*amūlikā-śraddhā-kṣānti*). He then resolved to provide a daily meal for a thousand monks. After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa...

Desiring to compile the Dharma-piṭaka, he intended to go forth on almsround; however, fearing that wicked heretics might pose difficult questions and thereby obstruct or waste his time, he concluded it would be better to accept King Aśoka’s offering of one thousand shares.

He then assembled one thousand arhats and compiled the teachings at the Vaiśālī Cave (Vebhāra-guhā). From this point on, the Teaching remained and was maintained in the world. King Aśoka constructed eighty-four thousand [stūpas].
There were four thousand jeweled stupas, and eighty-four thousand people were ordained as monks;
from this time forth, there have been tonsured and dyed-robed monks who maintain the world and follow the Three Jewels.

One must know that these Three Jewels are not some separate dharma, but are merely spoken of collectively after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; because there were three [Jewels] during the Buddha’s lifetime, they exist now through his passing.
The latter three [perfections] are therefore called "mutually following. These all pertain to the phenomenal level (*vastu*).
As the Treatise says: "As when I was formerly King Kali," and so forth.
This is because by abiding in the principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), one feels neither sorrow nor vexation; hence it is said: "At that time, there was no self or person."
This refers to the mark of equality (*samasamalakṣaṇa*). Since one abides in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), that true mark is itself without marks; hence it is said "and without marks" (*animitta*).
Being without marks means not being non-marks: there is no mark of saṃsāra and no mark of nirvāṇa, because one is free from the two extremes. Therefore, it is also said "nor is it non-mark."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites Kātyāyanīputra and others.

Kātyāyanīputra, relying on the *Āgama* sūtras, asserts that Bodhisattvas do not sever their afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and the hundred great kalpas.
This refers to Kātyāyanīputra himself, who, being of sharp faculties and great intelligence, did not study the Mahāyāna sūtras and was thus not a Great Bodhisattva.
For this reason, Nāgārjuna refutes [the Sarvāstivāda] throughout the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, as when he states:

"To say that a bodhisattva does not sever the fetters (saṃyojana) is called a great error," and so forth. Thus, since Pūrṇa (Canyan) bases his claim that a bodhisattva does not sever the fetters upon the *Āgama* sūtras, his position has scriptural authority.
This is why Jingxi said: "Since the *Āgamas* state that a bodhisattva does not sever [the fetters]..."

As for the statement that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) refutes the provisional [teachings], this does not mean they are entirely non-existent; rather, it is because there is also the principle that bodhisattvas do not sever their fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The criticism regarding "attachment" does not imply that such things are completely absent. However, Kātyāyanīputra was not appropriate in relying exclusively on the Hīnayāna teachings;
therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refuted him in various places, which was merely to refute his biased adherence to the Hīnayāna.
Within this, there is a brief explanation of four kinds of eyes.

The commentary provides two interpretations: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed analysis. In the detailed analysis, there are four kinds of eyes, all of which are based upon the five eyes.
The inclusion of form (*rūpa*) further consists of two kinds:
mundane knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and ultimate knowledge (*paramārtha-jñāna*). Question: Why does the treatise further distinguish these two kinds of knowledge within the inclusion of form?
Answer: There are two intentions. First, to demonstrate that phenomena (*dharma*) are necessarily identical with principle (*tattva*); second, [to show that]...
This is because the two wisdoms are of one essence. Indeed, these two meanings are in reality but one intention, for the phenomenon (*dharma*) is identical to the principle (*tattva*).
Thus, the two truths are of one essence. Regarding the first meaning: form (*rūpa*) is the phenomenon; within it, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is disclosed.

As for "principle," it reveals that the phenomenon must be identical to the principle. If the phenomenon were not identical to the principle, then mundane wisdom regarding the nine realms would be inverted.

"Transforms. The *Treatise* states: "By virtue of the power of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) transforms without inversion. Because it is identical to that principle (*tattva*), it transforms without inversion.

Regarding "the two knowledges being of one essence": this refers to the fact that, in terms of perfect expression, the entities of phenomena (*vastu*) and their principles (*tattva*) are of one essence.
Because mundane wisdom is entirely ultimate wisdom, and ultimate wisdom is entirely mundane wisdom;

although these two types of wisdom are distinguished, they truly have no dual substance. They are essentially one body that is mutually identical. Therefore, within the single dharma subsumed under form—
This explains these two kinds. It is like waves and water: the entire wave is water, and the entire water is the wave; although waves and water are distinct, they are not two.

One must know that the five eyes are the dharma-gate realized by the Buddha of Actual Fruit (Buddhatva), which the Bodhisattva Asanga explained through a fourfold analysis of the five eyes. Although the text is concise, its meaning is comprehensive.

The subtle and exhaustive perfection of its essential meaning accords with what is taught by the Tiantai school today; were it not for the fact that his internal realization was fundamentally identical to what he surveyed, how could he have reached such a state? It is truly lamentable.

Regarding "the fruit of the cultivation of the dharma-realm" and so forth: the dharma-realm refers to the ten dharma-realms. The "fruit" is called the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*). Cultivation pertains to phenomena (*vastu*);

because the five eyes have coarse objects, they are subsumed under form (*rūpa*). As for the ten realms: the two eyes of flesh and heaven pertain to the six realms of ordinary beings; the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) pertains to the two vehicles.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): the Dharma-eye is the realm of the Bodhisattva, and the Buddha-eye is the realm of the Buddha. Question:
If the Buddha-eye is explained by means of the ten realms, how can the lower realms, such as those of the hells and so forth, be used to explain the Buddha-eye? Answer:
Because the fruits of the ten dharma-realms are in fact fully possessed by the five eyes of the Buddha-fruit, the five eyes are explained in relation to the ten dharma-realms.
Therefore, it cannot be hindered or obstructed by the lower realms such as the various hells. Thus, the *Zhiguan* states: "The Buddha possesses the five eyes;
how could the retributive fruits of humans and devas be explained as the Buddha-eye? The *Fuxing* commentary explains this by saying: "This cites a single fruit of Buddhahood."
It is endowed with the ten realms; however, one must not equate the "saintly aggregates" (the term *āyatana* here refers to the fruit) with those of ordinary beings.
Thus, while the Buddha-fruit can indeed possess all ten realms, one must never take the Buddha’s hell-realm to be the same as the hell-realm of ordinary beings when explaining the Buddha-eye.
If this is so, and since all ten realms belong to the Buddha-fruit, by what means are they designated? One should know this.
Since the ten realms are already fully possessed through the fruit of Buddhahood, they receive their designation from that fruit of Buddhahood.

As for "the virtues of the fruit," these are the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. As Jingxi said: "When the two thousand [qualities] are perfected as the fruit, they are all designated as permanence and bliss."

Is this not what is meant? The three thousand realms are the ten dharma-realms; yet, if one does not grasp the ancestral intent of our present school, the treatise will remain obscure and its meaning hidden.
The term "treatise" (śāstra) refers to what precedes;

it points specifically to the five eyes mentioned in the preceding sutra text. This is for the purpose of clarifying the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the ultimate meaning (paramārtha), which is the primary truth.
Since this has already been explained and need not be restated here, it is referred back to what was previously stated.
It is subsumed within the truths of the three periods of time.
This is not explained in the treatise; however, as for the primary meaning of the sequence, it is because of the differentiation made by conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Thus, although the Buddha’s fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is the same as what ordinary beings see, the Buddha transcends what they see. The Buddha’s divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is the same [as that of others].
That which is seen by devas is surpassed by what the Buddha sees; this is what is called the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

The Buddha’s wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) perceives emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in the same manner as the two vehicles, yet it surpasses what they see. The Buddha’s dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) perceives the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) in the same manner as bodhisattvas.

Yet the Buddha transcends what is seen by those [others]. The Buddha’s Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus) illuminates all things perfectly and without partiality; as it encounters the five distinct objects of perception, it consequently possesses five functions, which are called the five eyes (pañca-cakṣuḥ).
One knows this to be a Buddha by means of the dharma of bodhi.
The dharma of bodhi refers to the dharma of the equality of the ten realms and the three truths; only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly manifest it.
Because they do not undergo suffering and affliction,
but instead enjoy the wealth and pleasures of humans and devas,
they naturally understand for themselves that these are aggregates and so forth, even if it is not explicitly taught.
Although it does not explicitly state that they are a multitude of atoms, one naturally knows them to be such. As for the purpose of this aggregation, it must be explained:
it is spoken in order to manifest the meaning of emptiness as a skillful means of non-perception; that is to say, they are "not" a multitude of atoms.
In the higher [stages], one contemplates only name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth.
In the higher [stages], one deals only with matter and the bodies of sentient beings. Within the contemplation of the "lump" (*piṇḍa-graha*), one refutes associated formations;

this is the combined explanation of name-and-form and the body, without further differentiating the "lump. Herein, for the sake of refuting false retribution, [one examines] that which is outside of name-and-form.

It is distinguished from the body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Therefore, it is separately identified as "lump-grasping" (*piṇḍagrāha*). Thus, when it is said that the world is substantially existent, this refers precisely to the "unified aggregate" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).
Now, this unified aggregate is empty. Yet, one does not realize that it is merely a combination of the four aggregates and the massing together of various particles;
to call such a thing a "unified aggregate" is surely not true reality. It is in this way that name-and-form is revealed.

The retribution of the body can be dispelled through the emotions. Therefore, Subhūti, for the purpose of establishing the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), spoke of the "unified aggregate" (*piṇḍa-grāha*).
The World-Honored One, in order to fulfill what Śakra had said, stated that it is precisely not an unified aggregate.
If wisdom knows by relying upon *śamatha*, then *śamatha*—which here is translated as "stopping"—is that which, through stopping, halts distraction; it is stillness within movement.
One does not know when there is distracted agitation, but one is able to know when there is tranquility.
One sees by relying on *vipaśyanā*; this [term] is translated as "seeing.
It is through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) that one is able to see; that is to say, by means of contemplation one contemplates the turbid.
As for that which is turbid, it is immediately [the state of] darkness; when dark, one does not see, but when bright, one is able to see. My ancestor said: "Luminous stillness" (*mingjing*).
This is the essence of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Thus, through the meditative equipoise of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one comes to know and see the true principle.

It is not that one cannot know it without seeing the truth; rather, by seeing the true principle, one is able to realize and know it. Therefore, regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), there is no conceptual discrimination.
*Caimei*. Where there were deficiencies in the arguments or omissions in the text, I have revised them once more to supplement what remained unexplained.

My humble efforts are intended solely to establish a virtuous karmic connection with Prajñāpāramitā. Written by Tanying in the second month of summer in the sixth year of the Qiandao era, the *gengyin* year of the sexagenary cycle.
